newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian business groups urge U.S. certification.
newsitem.headline: Colombian business groups urge U.S. certification.

text.p: Business leaders appealed to the United States on Wednesday to recognise Colombia's efforts in the war on drugs and stop treating it like "a banana republic."
The appeal came as government officials and business leaders wrapped up weeks of intense lobbying efforts to convince the United States to "certify" Colombia as an ally in the drug war.

The business groups said political factors, particularly allegations that President Ernesto Samper's 1994 election campaign was drug-financed, were the main obstacles to getting Colombia off Washington' virtual blacklist of "decertified" countries seen as not doing enough to fight drug trafficking.

"Decertifying Colombia because Samper is president is an unacceptable act," a top business group called the Union Intergremial Nacional said in a statement. It added that the country's victories -- on the legal front and on the ground -- in the war against drugs cannot be overlooked simply because the United States would like to see Samper forced out of power.

Samper was absolved by Congress last year of charges that he knowingly received millions of dollars in drug money to finance his campaign. Alluding to that decision, and to the fact that Samper has clung to office despite repeated calls for his resignation, the statement said: "Colombia is not a banana republic that can forcefully change institutions or public offices that don't work."
In an annual report to Congress, U.S. President Bill Clinton must say by March 1 whether Colombia should remain on the "decertified" list.
Juan Manuel Ospina, head of another powerful group, the National Business Council, said, "The political component (in certification) is called Ernesto Samper, there's no denying it."

He and Jorge Ramirez Ocampo, head of the National Exporters' Association said Colombia's blacklisting had hurt foreign investment flows over the past year and was penalising honest Colombians unfairly.

The business groups added that it would be hypocritical if Colombia were decertified and Mexico, which has been rocked by numerous drug scandals over the past year, is certified simply because of its economic importance to Washington under the North American Free Trade Agreement.

"Objective facts demonstrate that Mexico hasn't achieved even half of the results (in the anti-drug fight) that Colombia has shown over the last 12 months," the Union Intergremial Nacional statement said.
Decertification for a second consecutive year could trigger punitive economic sanctions that Clinton stopped short of imposing last year.

Apart from higher tariffs on Colombian exports to the United States, Clinton could invoke the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose a wide variety of sanctions, including the suspension of banking services between the United States and Colombia.

Few Colombians, in or outside the government, expect Washington to clamp sanctions on the country. But they say anything short of full certification, or decertification with a national security waiver, would be a serious injustice and put an enormous strain on U.S.-Colombia ties.

A high-ranking government official, who called the entire certification process "a bad neighbour policy" in remarks to foreign journalists early on Wednesday, warned that U.S.-Colombia ties would suffer dramatically if Colombia is decertified again this week.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, declined to spell out how relations would be affected. But reprisals could be taken against U.S. interests in Colombia, if economic sanctions were to affect Colombian businesses, and the government could move to curb covert U.S. anti-drug operations.
"There has to be a recognition of Colombia's (anti-drug) efforts," the official said. "And that recognition should be conditional certification."
